entries.title: What’s the Point of Running as a Republican in D.C.?
entries.summary: For this year's candidates, the reasons range from rodents to education to a need to challenge the status quo.
entries.content:
If you’re surprised to learn that a Puerto Rico-born immigration lawyer is running for local office in D.C. as a Republican, you’re probably not alone.

“I am probably one of the most unconventional Republicans you will meet,” admits Manuel Rivera.

Rivera wasn’t even a Republican until the last presidential election. Before that, he was a lifelong Democrat — a conservative one, by his own telling — who once mounted an unsuccessful bid for a seat in the Rhode Island House of Representatives.

But now he’s flying the Republican flag, and running for D.C. attorney general.

Rivera is one of seven like-minded Republican candidates vying for local office in D.C. this year, a slate that includes other similarly convention-bucking contenders. For example, a self-proclaimed Biblical Christian woman is challenging the D.C. Council chairman, who has been in office longer than she’s been alive. And a Republican will be on the ballot in Ward 1 — considered the city’s most progressive ward — for the first time in 16 years.

“This election is especially important because it represents a renewed effort by the Republican Party to offer the District’s voters a range of ideas and qualified candidates,” Rivera told The Washington Sun. “We have assembled one of the strongest Republican slates in history.”
Manuel Riviera (7792x5195, AR: 1.50)But for as strong as Rivera may think that slate is, so too are the local currents working against it. There hasn’t been a Republican elected to office in D.C. for almost two decades, and President Donald Trump’s vote share in the 2024 election barely exceeded 6%.

“It’s pointless,” said David Krucoff, who ran for the Ward 3 council seat as a moderate Republican in 2022 — notching a respectable 22% of the vote. He later became disillusioned with the party and is now an independent.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Still, turnout in the June Republican primary was higher than it has been in 14 years, a sign party leaders say is an indication of renewed local energy in the face of an inescapably tough political landscape. And many Republicans concede that even with victory unlikely, the value in running is just to offer voters something different.

“Washington, D.C. is a one-party system,” says Rivera. “I believe democracy works best when voters have a real choice. Somebody must be willing to challenge that status quo.”

Crime, Rodents and Education

The conventional wisdom in D.C. is that Rivera’s chances — like those of his fellow GOP candidates — aren’t very good in November.

Beyond the raw political reality that only 5% of the city’s 485,000 registered voters are Republicans, the party’s national brand has been on a downward trajectory in urban areas over the last three decades. There hasn’t been a Republican elected to the council since 2008.

“If you want to be a local Republican in D.C. now and generally are affiliated with the administration, that’s just not a popular thing to be,” said Krucoff.

Still, Rivera and the other GOP contenders say that D.C. voters are sophisticated enough to look past party labels. And D.C. voters certainly have in the past: In 1994, Carol Schwartz, a Republican member of the council, scored 42% of the vote against Marion Barry in the city’s mayoral race.

“Public safety, government accountability, taxes, and protecting our citizens are not just Republican or Democrat issues,” said Rivera. “They are D.C. residents’ issues.”

The main issue that animates almost all of the GOP contenders in D.C. is public safety — which has also been a primary focus of Trump’s, who last year deployed the National Guard in the city and frequently touts his successes on bringing down crime rates.
DC0A3210 copy.jpg (7403x4936, AR: 1.50)
“People don’t care if you’re from the left or the right. I tell them I am a Republican, that might jar them a bit, but I say, ‘Hey, what’s your biggest issue?’ And they say public safety,” said Jett Jasper, a candidate for the Ward 1 seat on the council, who says he would focus on increasing hiring for the Metropolitan Police Department.

Jorge Rice, who is running in Ward 6, says his emphasis on public safety comes from personal experience — he was assaulted on the D.C. streetcar in 2024, leaving him with a broken nose. “It made me want to take action,” he said.

In Ward 5, Jeff Kihien says it was rats in his backyard — as bipartisan a complaint as there is in D.C. — that motivated his own decision to run. “Washington D.C. is the capital of the United States, of the most powerful country on the whole planet, but we cannot solve the basic problem of rodents,” he said.

Kihien — who immigrated to the U.S. from Peru — also said he supports a “family wage” that would allow one half of every married couple to stay home instead of having to work.

Darrell Green, a former D.C. police officer who is running for an at-large council seat, is focused on one thing: “Education, education, education.” He thinks D.C. needs to do more to battle high truancy and absenteeism in schools. Abi Prudent, a candidate for council chair, is similarly interested in schools, primarily in preserving the IMPACT teacher assessment tool that some Democratic officials and activists have said they want to scrap.

“It’s hard for me to understand why we’d want to take away something that’s benefitting kids,” she said.

Denise Rosado, who is running to be D.C.’s non-voting delegate to Congress, would de-emphasize the city’s fight for statehood, instead pushing to exempt residents from paying federal taxes. As for Rivera, he criticizes incumbent Attorney General Brian Schwalb for “filing a lot of flashy lawsuits and some of them are settling for pennies on the dollar.”

‘The Hard Route’

The goal for the Republican candidates in D.C. seems clear: Don’t let Trump dominate the conversation. None of them fully shy away from Trump; they will say they voted for the president, but just as quickly point out where they disagree with him.

“It’s to the benefit of the voter you are talking about issues that you would have control over, and those are local issues like trash and recycling and rats and schools and the local budget,” said Carolina Celnik, the executive director of the D.C. GOP.

Still, there’s often significant overlap in D.C. between what happens on the local and federal levels — largely because the city is often beholden to the whims of Congress and the White House.

In that, the D.C. Republican Party has evolved over the years. It was once consistently in favor of Congress letting District residents and their elected officials determine their own fate; it even gave a nod towards the eventual goal of D.C. statehood. Now, Celnik says, local Republicans are content with the newly aggressive role that Capitol Hill is playing in local politics.

“They are doing what they are doing for the benefit of D.C. residents,” she said. “It’s honestly kind of embarrassing that the federal government has had to step in and do for the city what the city should have been doing for itself.”
DC0A2993 copy.jpg (6988x4659, AR: 1.50)D.C. voters, though, may disagree. A Washington Post poll conducted over the summer found that 79% of respondents said they opposed Trump’s aggressive involvement in local issues.

But given that the GOP has become so enmeshed in the city’s local affairs, the Republican candidates say they could serve as a friendly conduit between the White House, Congress and local officials.

“We should have a better relationship with the federal government and White House,” said Rivera. “As a Republican… I can build that bridge.”

Krucoff, the former Republican, thinks there is space for right-leaning candidates in D.C. Starting in 2028, independent voters — and there are roughly 80,000 of them — will be able to cast ballots in either the Republican or Democratic primary. That, he says, could open a path for a conservative contender while avoiding the political baggage of being associated with the GOP brand.

“It has never been a better time for anyone who sees themselves as center or right of center to become active in D.C. politics as an unaffiliated voter,” he said.

For D.C.’s local Republican candidates, though, the focus now is more pedestrian: They need to knock on doors and meet voters, as well as raise money. In that, another very real challenge emerges. As of last month, for one, Rivera had just over $10,000 in his campaign’s account. Schwalb, the Democratic incumbent, had $821,000. Prudent had roughly $2,300; Chairman Phil Mendelson, the incumbent, had $87,000.

Nonetheless, Prudent remains upbeat about the challenge she has assigned herself.

“Yes, I have allowed myself to take this campaign the hard route by running as a Republican,” she said. “But what’s most important for me is not trying to make things happen the easy way and trying to convince people to vote for me because of a letter that’s next to my name.”

entries.title: To Overhaul His Game, Frances Tiafoe Came Home
entries.summary: Tiafoe’s new routine included some hitting sessions with Ben Shelton, who he’ll face Friday in the U.S. Open semifinals.
entries.content:
Frances Tiafoe finished last season looking for a fresh start. It had been a decade since he turned pro, and despite flashes of brilliance and occasionally deep tournament runs, he’d found himself stalling and skidding through 2025. So he overhauled his approach. Tiafoe skipped most of the Asian and European competitions that round out the annual tennis calendar. He used the autumn to find a new coach and start a new practice regimen. And rather than relocating somewhere new or heading somewhere warm, Tiafoe instead went home to Maryland, training for roughly six weeks at the facility where he discovered the sport as a child in College Park, the Junior Tennis Champions Center.

He sometimes brought a very recognizable hitting partner.

Ben Shelton also spent time in the D.C. area this offseason. He is dating Washington Spirit star Trinity Rodman. Over the last few years on the ATP Tour, the 23-year-old Shelton and 28-year-old Tiafoe have been competitors, but they have grown into a friendship, too. It only made sense that, on multiple occasions, Shelton joined Tiafoe at JTCC.

The two elite talents mixed in with the ordinary hum of the surrounding courts. “It's a treat to have two players of that level, practicing in front of all of our kids and members,” says JTCC CEO Martin Blackman. “It was really special.”

The pair will play again this weekend on a somewhat bigger stage.

Friday night, Tiafoe and Shelton will meet in the U.S. Open semifinals. It will be their third time playing at the tournament in the last four years. (Shelton won in the quarterfinals in 2023; Tiafoe got revenge in the third round in 2024.) Each player is seeking his first Grand Slam final and, by extension, a chance to become the first American man to win a major since Andy Roddick in 2003. There will be a watch party, naturally, at JTCC.

Tiafoe and Shelton hit together at the facility at least three times as they prepped for this season, Blackman says. (JTCC posted a video of one such joint training session last November.) It was part of an unusually intense offseason at the facility for Tiafoe.

His relationship with the place has always been special. Nearly every match of his includes some commentary about his origin story and, in turn, his connection with JTCC: When he was a toddler, his father worked on the labor crew that built the facility, and that construction job became a maintenance role after the courts opened. From a young age, Tiafoe was surrounded by tennis, growing up around the facility and taking advantage of every opportunity he could find there. The son of Sierra Leonean immigrants became a prodigy and then a pro.

Like many tennis players, he established a base in Florida, where he generally spends his winters. But last offseason, searching for a way to shake up his career, Tiafoe decided that most of his training should happen back home in Maryland.
Frances Tiafoe (1956x1304, AR: 1.50)For years, Tiafoe had seemed perpetually on the verge of a breakthrough, always talented but never quite consistent. A strong run through 2023 and ’24 had faded into a lackluster 2025. He decided that something had to change. Tiafoe brought on a new coach, Mark Kovacs, with a focus on data and sports science.

“We all know he could play tennis at a high level,” Kovacs told the ATP Tour’s website in January. “Now it's about, ‘Can he take care of the little details on a daily basis?’” That meant everything from his fitness to his serve mechanics to his arrival time at the facility. (Kovacs is a stickler for punctuality.) They refined his diet and maximized his sleep. And on the same courts where he learned the game as a kid, Tiafoe worked to unlock a new level of performance as an adult.

“It was every day,” says Blackman, who originally worked at JTCC when Tiafoe was in elementary school and returned to run the center last year. “I mean, day in and day out.”

This was a striking change in approach for Tiafoe. It was immediately obvious in some ways: He lost 17 pounds. That kind of work does not always translate directly to better results on the court. Yet here it did. Tiafoe was in better shape, yes, but he was also more clear-minded about what he was chasing and it would ask of him.

“There’s a lot of things I've changed,” Tiafoe said at the French Open in May. “Just having a lot of conversations, trying to be real, man. What are you really trying to do? What are you trying to get out of it? You know, just stop hiding behind your talent, stop hiding behind the gift. … A lot of times you can get away with stuff because you're so gifted. But use the gift the right way, and, you know, squeeze a lemon and see what you can get out of it.”

Tiafoe began the season ranked No. 32. He now sits higher than ever at No. 8. He won his first ATP 500 trophy at the Terra Wortmann Open in June, and for just the second time in his career, has made it to at least the third round of all four Grand Slams. But his best performance of all has come over the last two weeks at the U.S. Open.

It has always been his favorite major — on home soil, in front of a traditionally loud, rambunctious crowd that matches his energy — and he has played like it.

Tiafoe cruised into the quarterfinals. He then dropped the first two sets to Alex Michelsen. It was a match that he might have easily lost a year ago — a match that nearly anyone would have lost at that point. Yet it was not a match that Tiafoe lost in 2026. He gutted out a remarkable comeback, winning 5-7, 3-6, 7-5, 6-3, 7-6 (6), and promptly offered a touching display of sportsmanship by interrupting his own celebration to embrace a distraught Michelsen. That good cheer has always been a signature of his. But that particular brand of gritty, persistent tennis represented something new.

“The match against Michelsen, I think, is almost kind of the epitome of the difference in him now,” Blackman says. “He knows that as long as he’s in the match, he’s got a chance, because he’s always making adjustments, he’s fit enough to go the distance, and he’s got the belief that he can stand on the work that he did.”

Back at JTCC, where so much of that work took place, they were all watching. And they'll be watching again Friday night, as a familiar pairing faces off somewhere different.

entries.title: U.S. Inflation Accelerates as Gas Prices Continue to Climb
entries.summary: The figures show that inflation remains stubbornly elevated, more than five years after prices first soared as the economy emerged from the COVID pandemic.
entries.content:
By Christopher Rugaber

WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. inflation accelerated last month as gas prices spiked in the wake of renewed fighting in the Middle East, underscoring the affordability challenges that are top of mind for many voters with midterm elections now just seven weeks away.

The consumer price index rose 3.4% last month compared with a year ago, the Labor Department said Friday, the same as in July. But on a monthly basis, inflation quickened, as costs jumped 0.4% from July to August, up from an increase of just 0.1% the previous month.

The figures show that inflation remains stubbornly elevated, more than five years after prices first soared as the economy emerged from the COVID pandemic. Persistent inflation has presented a major challenge for the inflation-fighters at the Federal Reserve and has soured many voters on the Trump administration’s economic track record.

Excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core prices were 2.4% higher in August than a year ago, down slightly from July's 2.5% and the third straight decline. But on a monthly basis, core prices rose 0.3% from July to August, the largest increase since April.

The larger-than-expected monthly increase in core prices will likely embolden those Fed officials who have pushed for the central bank to lift its benchmark interest rate at its meeting next week. Wall Street investors now see about 70% likelihood the Fed will increase rates Sept. 16, according to CME Fedwatch.

The Trump administration is seeking to counter voter concerns about high prices and rising interest rates as the midterm elections approach. President Donald Trump on Wednesday promised $5,000 payments to every American adult if the GOP keeps a majority in Congress, a move that would require congressional approval and could stoke inflation. And Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has stepped up buybacks of Treasury bonds in an effort to keep longer-term interest rates lower. Yet on Thursday the yield on the 10-year Treasury reached a nearly three-year high.

Renewed fighting in the Middle East has pushed up energy costs, with the nationwide average cost of a gallon of gas on Friday jumping more than 7% from a month ago to $4.30.

Hotel room prices and airfares also rose last month while new and used cars got more expensive. Apparel and grocery prices were unchanged from July to August.

Inflation as one-time shock, or something more

Many economists and Federal Reserve officials have long considered higher gas prices one of several “one-time” shocks that are lifting inflation, along with tariffs and surging investment in AI data centers. For months, the hope has been that as the war against Iran wound down, and the effects of tariffs faded, inflation would grind lower.

Yet there are few signs of the Iran war cooling, and even Trump has said gas prices won't retreat until after the midterm elections in November. And while Trump's trade fight with Canada will impact a small number of imports, it is a reminder that tariffs remain a threat that could push up other costs.

“This is not one and done,” said Kathy Bostjancic, chief economist at Nationwide. “It's unclear when tensions in the Middle East are going to settle down. ... This seems like it could be a prolonged disruption.”

While core prices are rising more slowly than overall prices, more expensive oil and gas could spread through more of the economy. Pricier jet fuel will likely push up airfares, and more expensive diesel will raise shipping costs, which could make groceries and other goods shipped by truck more expensive. On Thursday, a wholesale price report showed a jump in chemical prices, likely a result of more expensive oil.

What will the Federal Reserve do?

Federal Reserve policymakers are split on whether to hike at a meeting next week, so much so that differences of a few hundredths of a percentage point in Friday's inflation report could determine whether the central bank boosts its benchmark interest rate or leaves it unchanged. The Fed, which is tasked with keeping inflation in check, typically lifts borrowing costs to slow spending and limit price increases.

Investors and analysts differ over whether the Fed will hike rates at their Sept. 15-16 meeting. Chair Kevin Warsh suggested he was leaning toward a rate hike in a high-profile speech two weeks ago, but he did not commit to doing so at a specific time.

And last Thursday, Fed governor Christopher Waller, echoing some other Fed officials, suggested that if Friday’s inflation report shows price increases cooling, then he would support keeping rates where they are. Waller is one of the 12 officials who vote on each Fed rate decision.

Waller's heavy emphasis on August's figures has raised the stakes for Friday's report. If the monthly core figure rounds up to 0.3%, some Wall Street analysts expect the Fed would then hike rates. But if it rounded down to 0.2% or lower, then a hold could be more likely. If it is somewhere in between, it's not clear what the Fed may do. One analyst called such considerations “ludicrous precision.”

For his part, Warsh doesn't want to tip his hand about his next moves, which some economists say will make this kind of uncertainty more common before Fed meetings.
